author: Evan Ochsner

Its implementation examples support feasibility, while its caution about uncertain pricing and competitive effects is consistent with the cluster’s rejection of a single predetermined market outcome.
qs: # Law Firms Capitalize on Internal Data to Stand Out in AI Age  *Evan Ochsner — Bloomberg Law (2026)*  Large law firms are meeting the AI moment with a new strategy: use that advanced tech to mobilize their rich, internal data trove as a competitive advantage.

“They will need that path, because AI tools are increasingly allowing firms to deliver more of the same work in fewer billable six-minute increments than they log today.”  Still, it’s not yet clear what this AI future will look like or to what extent AI will actually change the business of law.

It documents substantial investments and partnerships but does not claim demonstrated returns, and it does not materially address the cluster’s broader hiring uncertainty.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s core claims that competitive differentiation may come from proprietary knowledge and customised workflows rather than access to underlying models, and that sourcing is a portfolio choice combining external tools with internal development. Its Kirkland and Polsinelli examples also preserve the cluster’s caution that investment and deployment do not yet prove durable superiority.
qs: The firms that have chosen to customize AI have determined their data will make them stand out against peers in a world where every law firm can buy the same tech.

kp.k: Proprietary knowledge becomes firms’ proposed competitive advantage
kp.d: The article reports that large firms are betting on AI-enabled use of internal knowledge, rather than hours billed, as a source of enduring value in areas including private equity fundraising and M&A. Factor’s Nicole Bradick predicts that extracting employees’ knowledge will become the decisive differentiator; this is a strategic expectation, not an established market outcome.
qs: Firms in this camp are betting that their enduring value won’t be measured in hours billed, but in the unique knowledge an individual firm’s attorneys have.

“The only thing that is going to be a competitive differentiator into the future—the only thing that is going to matter—is how you extract and leverage the knowledge of the people who work within the firm,” said Nicole Bradick, global head of innovation at the legal services company Factor.

kp.k: Firms customize shared models with institutional expertise
kp.d: Reported examples include Clifford Chance and Crowell & Moring building on OpenAI’s GPT, Freshfields collaborating with Anthropic, and Fried Frank using historically well-structured data for private funds tools. The article presents these efforts as attempts to distinguish firms when competitors can purchase the same technology, rather than evidence of demonstrated performance improvements.
qs: Clifford Chance and Crowell & Moring have both built on top of OpenAI’s GPT.
Freshfields is collaborating with Anthropic to develop “novel AI legal workflows.”
Fried Frank is using a long history of well-structured data to build tools that will generate more efficient work for its private funds clients.
“What sets us apart if everything we use AI for is on a third-party tool that’s available to everyone?” Asay said.

kp.k: Kirkland commits major funding and specialist hiring
kp.d: Kirkland & Ellis has committed $500 million over three or four years to AI capabilities marketed to clients and is seeking dozens of AI and legal technology innovation employees. Its chairman said hundreds of attorneys contributed input. The article reports a private equity fundraising platform launch, but explicitly leaves the depth of Kirkland’s technical development uncertain and considers its own large language model unlikely.
qs: Kirkland’s half-billion dollar investment will stretch out over three or four years.

The firm’s chairman suggested the AI investment will allow for the expansion of billing models other than the billable hour and that the firm used input from hundreds of its attorneys to build the tool.
On Thursday, the firm launched a platform for private equity fundraising it said is “built around Kirkland’s institutional knowledge, workflows and legal judgment.”
How far Kirkland will push into the technical side of building AI is unclear.

kp.k: Buying and limited customization remain alternative strategies
kp.d: The article describes firms choosing among buying, building, or combining both approaches. Polsinelli has deployed Thomson Reuters’ CoCounsel and an enterprise ChatGPT subscription while developing custom capabilities around them. Its chief operating officer, Regan Lemke, distinguishes that approach from competing with big technology companies.
qs: They can buy artificial intelligence tools, build their own, or a combination of both.
Polsinelli, for example, has rolled out Thomson Reuters’ CoCounsel and an enterprise subscription to ChatGPT.
It’s developing custom capabilities around those tools, but not trying to compete against big tech, chief operating officer Regan Lemke said.
“We’re a law firm. We’re not a tech shop,” Lemke said.

kp.k: Direct vendor sales raise prospective competitive threats
kp.d: The article reports that Harvey and Legora increasingly pitch directly to corporate legal departments. Purple co-founder Dom Conte argues that firms’ purchases and collaborations teach vendors legal workflows and could create future competitors. The article suggests proprietary AI might mitigate this threat if successful; neither vendor commented, and displacement is not established.
qs: Tools like Harvey and Legora are increasingly pitching themselves directly to corporate legal departments, posing a potential problem for law firms’ businesses.
Firms have essentially shown the AI startups what legal workflows look like by buying those tools and collaborating with them, Conte said.
“Basically you are building the competitor of the future by buying technology off the shelf,” he said.
Harvey and Legora declined to comment.

kp.k: Clients hope AI investment accelerates alternative pricing
kp.d: The article reports client hopes that firms’ AI investments will move billing away from hourly charges. Wayfair general counsel Enrique Colbert welcomed Kirkland’s announcement as progress toward ending the billable hour, while Kirkland’s chairman suggested the investment could expand other billing models. These are expectations rather than reported evidence of completed pricing changes.
qs: In-house leaders have long railed against the billable hour, and because law firms are investing in AI, clients hope they will move to other pricing models.

“It’s a few steps closer to killing the billable hour, which is where we all know we need to go,” Wayfair general counsel Enrique Colbert said in an email reacting to the Kirkland announcement. “It’s exciting.”

kp.k: Value-based billing depends on demonstrable client value
kp.d: Darktrace chief legal officer David Morris argues that firms must show AI improves legal quality to sustain earnings. He sees client-recognized, distinctive platforms as a more credible route to value-based billing because AI increasingly reduces the billable time needed for existing work. This is an attributed commercial assessment, not a quantified finding about productivity or revenue.
qs: In order for law firms to keep making money while using AI tools, they’re going to need to show clients those tools are actually enhancing the quality of legal work, said David Morris, chief legal officer of the cybersecurity company Darktrace.
“The firms that get this right can build platforms their clients recognize as genuinely unique and valuable, to give the firms a more credible path to value-based billing,” Morris said in an email.
“They will need that path, because AI tools are increasingly allowing firms to deliver more of the same work in fewer billable six-minute increments than they log today.”

kp.k: The extent of business transformation remains uncertain
kp.d: The article explicitly qualifies its account: the future form and magnitude of AI’s effects on the business of law remain unclear. Toshiba America Group chief legal officer Timothy Fraser describes the trend as early-stage, with participants still needing to work through its implications.
qs: Still, it’s not yet clear what this AI future will look like or to what extent AI will actually change the business of law.
“I look at this as an industry trend that we’re in the early stages of, and we’re all going to have to work our way through this,” said Timothy Fraser, chief legal officer of Toshiba America Group.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source presents proprietary knowledge, customized AI tools, competitive pressure from vendors, and changes to billing as interconnected developments in legal services.
pts.d: Evan Ochsner reports that large firms are using AI to turn internal data and expertise into a competitive advantage, betting that their value will increasingly reside in distinctive knowledge rather than hours billed. Factor's Nicole Bradick predicts that extracting employees' knowledge will be the decisive future differentiator. Crowell's Alma Asay argues that customized tools will distinguish firms as shared third-party tools become commonplace. Purple's Dom Conte predicts that legal-tech vendors selling directly to corporate legal departments will become competitors to firms, partly because firms have helped those vendors understand legal workflows. These are competitive predictions, not findings of demonstrated displacement. Ochsner reports that Kirkland's chairman suggested its AI investment would support billing models beyond hourly charging. Wayfair general counsel Enrique Colbert welcomes the investment as movement away from the billable hour. Darktrace chief legal officer David Morris says AI increasingly reduces the time needed for existing work and argues that firms must demonstrate enhanced quality and distinctive client value to sustain revenues through value-based billing. Polsinelli's Regan Lemke describes an alternative strategy: adopting third-party tools and customizing around them rather than competing with big tech.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of reported investments, deployments, collaborations, a platform launch, and practitioner assessments—not quantified tests of productivity, quality, or market outcomes.
pts.d: Ochsner cites Kirkland's $500 million commitment, input from hundreds of attorneys reported by its chairman, AI-related recruitment listed on its career board, and a private equity fundraising platform launch. Other examples include Clifford Chance and Crowell building on OpenAI's GPT, Freshfields collaborating with Anthropic, Fried Frank using structured historical data for private funds tools, and Polsinelli deploying CoCounsel and enterprise ChatGPT. These examples document investment and implementation strategies; they do not establish that customization has already produced competitive advantage or superior legal work. The predictions about differentiation and vendor competition rest on interviewed innovation leaders and an AI-tool builder. Billing expectations and requirements rest on corporate legal leaders' views. No measured time savings, quality comparisons, revenue effects, or vendor-driven loss of law-firm work are supplied. The article discloses that Bloomberg Law is itself a legal technology provider.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Implementation is already underway in the 2026 account, but competitive and pricing outcomes are mostly conditional, longer-term predictions without firm deadlines.
pts.d: Kirkland's investment is scheduled over three or four years. Asay places differentiation in the long run, while Conte says vendor competition will become a threat at some unspecified point. Ochsner explicitly conditions mitigation of vendor threats on the success of firms' strategies. Morris conditions a credible path to value-based billing on clients recognizing platforms as distinctive and valuable and on firms showing quality improvements. The extent of Kirkland's technical build remains unclear; the article says it is unlikely to build its own large language model and could instead build other AI or build on existing LLMs. Not every firm is choosing to build its own tools. Ochsner cautions that the eventual extent of business-model change remains unclear, and Toshiba America Group chief legal officer Timothy Fraser characterizes the trend as early-stage.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern large law firms, their corporate clients, legal-tech vendors, and personnel developing firms' AI capabilities.
pts.d: Large firms face choices about buying, building, and customizing AI, along with pressure to differentiate and preserve revenues as work requires fewer billable hours. Attorneys' accumulated expertise becomes an input into firm-specific tools. Private equity fundraising, private funds work, and M&A are identified as relevant practice areas. Corporate legal departments are both direct targets for vendors such as Harvey and Legora and buyers seeking improved quality and alternatives to hourly billing from firms. The vendors are described as potential competitive threats through direct sales to buyers, not as established alternative legal service providers delivering legal work. Kirkland's recruitment indicates demand for AI and legal-technology innovation personnel, but the source does not predict aggregate lawyer job losses or staffing restructuring. It does not make claims about access to justice or effects on the general public.
